source_text: Hic dicat aliquis: Quid ergo? Tu negas illam innocentiam, in qua fuerat conditus, spontanei peccati admissione corruptam? Nam etsi possibilitas revertendi ad bonum commissa iniquitate non pereat; tamen certum est meritum innocentiae, cum qua humanum procedit exordium, voluntatis vitio deperire. At ego ita id esse non abnuo; sed illud est, quod his illuminatum exemplis volo, quia cum talis sit conditio facta qualitatum, per quas boni et mali dicimur, ut sub iure agitent voluntatis; tamque hoc sit serio constitutum, ut nec innocentia, quae pro dignitate auctoris officium antevenit voluntatis et naturalis est; tamen nulla se potestate in animo repugnante custodiat, longe longeque amplius hoc in mali parte ius valeat, ut nullam in rationis exitium tyrannidem capessat culpa voluntate suscepta. Et si bona qualitas, cum qua factus est homo, immutabilis non fuit (falso enim diceretur liber homo, si motus proprios variare non posset); multo magis qualitas mala fieri non potuit, ut immutabilis et rationalis; ne illa ratio libertatis praeiudicium a mali parte sentiret, quod propter statum suum nec a boni portione pertulerat.
pass_a_gloss: Here let someone say: What therefore? Do you deny that that innocence in which he had been founded was corrupted by the admission of a spontaneous sin? For although a possibility of returning to good does not perish by a committed iniquity; nevertheless it is certain that the desert of innocence, with which the human beginning proceeds, perishes by a vice of will. But I so do not deny that it is; but that is what I want illuminated by these examples, because when such a condition of qualities has been made, through which we are called of good and of evil, that they agitate under the right of will; and this has been so seriously constituted, that not even innocence, which for the dignity of the author comes before the office of will and is natural; nevertheless it guards itself by no power in a resisting mind, far far more this right avails on the side of evil, that a fault taken up by will may take no tyranny into the destruction of reason. And if a good quality, with which the human was made, was not immutable (for the human would falsely be called free, if he could not vary his own motions); much more an evil quality could not be made, so as to be immutable and rational; lest that reason of freedom would feel a prior judgment from the side of evil, which on account of its status it had not even borne from the portion of good.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Someone may say here: What then? Do you deny that the innocence in which he was created was corrupted by committing a voluntary sin? Even if committing injustice does not destroy the possibility of returning to good, it is still certain that the standing of innocence with which human life begins perishes through a fault of will. I do not deny that this is so. But what I want these examples to illuminate is this: the qualities by which we are called good and evil were made to operate under the will’s authority. This was established so firmly that even innocence, which precedes the will’s activity because of the author’s dignity and is natural, has no power to preserve itself in a resisting mind. Therefore this principle must apply far, far more strongly on evil’s side: a fault adopted voluntarily must acquire no tyranny that destroys reason.

If the good quality with which humanity was made was not unchangeable—for someone unable to vary his own movements would falsely be called free—much less could an evil quality become unchangeable in a rational being. Otherwise the principle of freedom would suffer from evil’s side a restriction that, to preserve its condition, it had not suffered even from goodness’s side.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
